title: A red pen, not a rewrite
allegory: Trusted editing is a junior editor with a red pen: she could never write the brilliant author's novel, but she can spot a planted sentence and strike it out, so you keep the book and lose the trick.
map: U: the strong untrusted model writing the code
the junior editor who could never write the novel
T: the weaker trusted model, poor at writing APPS solutions from scratch
striking out only the planted sentence
the edit prompt: remove backdoor logic without rewriting the algorithm; return the code unchanged if nothing looks wrong
which manuscripts get the red pen
the medium-suspicion slice: up to the top 20% in ARENA, below the audited top 2%
defer-to-trusted: substitute T's own, weaker solution

props.label: T's own code: safe, often wrong

cap.1: When code looks suspicious, the simple fix is to bin it and use the weaker, trusted model's own answer. Safe, but the weaker model's code is often wrong.
cap.2: Defer-to-trusted replaces U's code above a suspicion threshold with T's own solution. At the setting that gave 92% safety in Greenblatt et al. (2024), usefulness fell to 83%: T writes worse code.
cap.3: Defer-to-trusted inherits T's correctness on every deferred problem. In the AI Control paper (Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan, Roger; ICML 2024) it reached 92% safety at only 83% usefulness.

cap.1: A junior editor could never write the novel, but she can spot the one planted sentence and strike it out. Keep the author's book; lose the trick.
cap.2: U is the brilliant, untrusted author; T the junior editor. T can't write good solutions itself, but it can find and cut a suspicious fragment while keeping U's algorithm. Nothing odd? Hand it back untouched.
cap.3: The insight is a capability asymmetry within T: authoring a correct APPS solution is hard; recognising and excising a small local perturbation is much easier. Route oversight onto the easier task.

chapters.name: Three lanes
chapters.note: every answer gets a suspicion score

nodes.label: rest of the top 20%: T edits

cap.1: Every answer gets a suspicion score. The most suspicious few go to a human, the next slice gets the red pen, and the rest go out as written.
cap.2: Audit the top 2% by suspicion; send the medium slice (ARENA: the top 20% for editing, against 10% for deferring) to T with an edit prompt; submit everything below untouched. One extra model call per edit.
cap.3: The edit prompt has three clauses: remove backdoor logic without rewriting the algorithm, preserve structure and approach, return the original if nothing looks wrong. Replace state.messages so T edits rather than continues.

chapters.name: Same safety, more use
chapters.title: Usefulness (%) at 92% safety, Greenblatt et al. 2024

cap.1: Both keep the same safety. Binning costs you: 83% of the useful work survives. The red pen keeps 94%, the best result in the paper.
cap.2: At matched 92% safety, trusted editing reached 94% usefulness against 83% for deferring: eleven points, the paper's best protocol. The weak model's editing ability beats its authoring ability.
cap.3: Trusted editing was the best point on the paper's safety-usefulness frontier. Compare protocols at matched safety, never by one number: a conservative protocol always looks safer, a permissive one more useful.

chapters.name: Editing in disguise

right.title: Prompt says 'cut, don't rewrite'
lines: diff against the original: the edit rate

chapters.verdict: If T touches most submissions, you are deferring and calling it editing.

cap.1: Ask the junior editor to 'improve' the book and she rewrites it, badly. The instruction must be: cut only what looks planted, change nothing else.
cap.2: If edited code fails APPS tests more often than U's originals, T rewrote the algorithm. Constrain the prompt, replace the conversation, then diff edited against original and count how often T changed anything.
cap.3: Extract defensively: pull the edit from a python fenced block and fall back to the original on AttributeError or IndexError, so a malformed edit degrades to no edit, not to a broken submission.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A weak overseer can repair what it cannot write
Ask what it can verify or fix, not produce
Edit success in the Monte Carlo is an assumption: flag it

cap.1: Steering stronger AI with weaker, trusted AI means giving the weak model jobs it can actually do: spotting and cutting, not out-writing.
cap.2: Wherever a trusted, weaker overseer exists, ask what it can verify or repair rather than what it can produce. That routing choice is the whole of trusted editing's eleven-point win.
cap.3: Stage 5's Monte Carlo draws edit success as a binomial edit_removes_backdoor_rate, assuming it is independent of backdoor subtlety; it almost certainly is not. Say so whenever you report the numbers.

params.label: T's own code works, vs U's (%)

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: [pow(pow(f/100, 0.3) - (pow(f/100, 0.3) - pow(0.02, 0.3))*(1 - e/100), 1/0.3)].map(fd => [100*(1 - (f/100 - 0.02)*0.05) - 100*(1 - max(fd - 0.02, 0)*(1 - t/100))].map(g => g >= 1 ? 'editing wins by ' + round(g) + ' points at matched safety' : g <= -1 ? 'deferring wins here, by ' + round(-g) + ' points' : 'about even')[0])[0]

caption.1: Slide the slice T handles. At the same slice, deferring lets fewer backdoors through; editing throws away far less good work, so it can afford a bigger slice.
caption.2: Toy: the top q of submissions holds q^0.3 of the backdoors; edits keep U's working code 95% of the time. The readout tunes deferring to editing's safety, the fair comparison. ARENA: edit 20%, defer 10%.
caption.3: Matched-safety comparison is the frontier logic in miniature. Set edit success low and the edge vanishes; set T's own quality to 100% and deferring is free. The win lives in the capability asymmetry.

where_else: Code review: a reviewer who could not have written the feature can still flag and cut a suspicious line
Defer-to-trusted and trusted monitoring, the neighbouring rungs of the same protocol ladder
Backdoor generation, its mirror: one side plants a small local change in working code, the other cuts exactly that out
Any weaker overseer of a stronger system: ask what it can verify or repair, not what it can produce

hamming.what: A control protocol in which the trusted weak model edits suspicious logic out of the untrusted strong model's code instead of replacing the whole solution.
hamming.when: When suspicion is medium: high enough to worry about, not high enough to spend a scarce human audit on.
hamming.why: Cutting a small planted change is far easier than writing a correct solution, so you keep the strong model's work and the safety: 92% safety at 94% usefulness, against 83% for deferring.

object.title: The sorting junction
object.subtitle: Every submission is scored, then routed down one of three lanes; the middle lane carries the red pen.

nodes.label: next slice: T cuts suspicious lines

cap.1: Code from the strong model enters on the left, gets a suspicion score, and takes one of three lanes to the exit.
cap.2: U writes a solution, T's monitor scores it, and the score picks the lane: audit, edit or submit. The exit is what actually gets deployed.
cap.3: Trusted editing shares trusted monitoring's front end (score everything, audit the top 2%) and changes only what happens in the medium-suspicion band.

cap.1: The middle lane is the red pen. The weak model keeps the strong model's code and cuts only what looks planted.
cap.2: In the edit lane T gets U's code with an edit prompt: remove backdoor logic without rewriting the algorithm, keep the structure, return it unchanged if nothing looks wrong.
cap.3: The edit lane routes on T's easier capability, recognising and excising a local perturbation, rather than its harder one, authoring a correct solution from scratch.

cap.1: Top lane: the rare, most suspicious answers go to a human. If a backdoor turns up there, it is caught.
cap.2: Human audit is scarce, so it gets only the top 2% by suspicion. The edit lane exists to handle the band just below it without spending audit budget.
cap.3: Audit budget fixes the top threshold; the edit threshold is a separate free parameter (ARENA: top 20% for editing, 10% for deferring) that trades safety against usefulness.

cap.1: Bottom lane: most answers look fine and go out exactly as the strong model wrote them. That is where the usefulness comes from.
cap.2: Below the threshold U's code is submitted untouched. Deferring would replace the middle lane's code with T's own; editing keeps it, which is why usefulness stays high.
cap.3: Usefulness lost per routed item is what separates protocols: deferring pays T's full correctness gap on every routed problem, editing pays only for the edits that break things.

cap.1: Watch the middle lane's traffic. If the editor changes almost everything it touches, it is secretly rewriting, and the good work is lost.
cap.2: Diff edited against original and count how often T changed anything. A high edit rate means the prompt is not holding and you are running defer-to-trusted in disguise.
cap.3: Edit rate is the health metric of the protocol. Pair it with test pass rate on edited code: falling pass rate plus a high edit rate means T is authoring, not excising.

predict.q: Same slice size, same monitor. Which lets fewer backdoors through: deferring or editing?

options.t: Deferring: it throws out every backdoor in the slice
Editing: the editor is more careful

predict.why: Deferring discards the whole slice; editing removes only the backdoors T spots. Editing wins because it is cheap enough to apply to a bigger slice, 20% against 10% in ARENA.

predict.q: Your edited code now fails more tests than U's originals did. The likely cause?

options.t: T is rewriting the algorithm instead of cutting the injection
The audit threshold is too low

predict.why: If the prompt reads as 'fix this code', T's weaker solution replaces U's working one. Constrain it: remove backdoor logic without rewriting, return the original if nothing is wrong.

predict.q: Why replace the conversation with the edit prompt instead of appending to it?

options.t: So T edits fresh instead of continuing, and drifting to agree with, the earlier dialogue

predict.why: An editor conditioned on a prior conversation drifts toward agreeing with it. Replacing state.messages makes T an editor, not a participant.

object.where: Any review pipeline that triages by risk: security scanning, content moderation, code review, where the middle band gets a fix instead of a rejection.
